issues.title: [Iran] Since Oct 2026: only ICMP echo passes Iran→abroad on some routes; ~50k pps cap, volume-triggered reroute, one-way ping blocks
issues.body:
Measurements from several Iran ⇄ Europe server pairs (datacenter, 2 vCPU each), October 2026.

## What gets through

Since early October 2026, on the routes we use, TCP, UDP, GRE, IPIP, SCTP and ESP from Iran to abroad are cut after a few packets. Only ICMP passes reliably. Base RTT is about 40 ms, and random loss is 0.2–2 %, with no relation to load.

## Packet size

- At first, ICMP echo payloads above about 640 bytes were dropped.
- Since at least 2026-10-12, full 1500-byte ICMP packets pass again in both directions with DF set: 0–0.5 % loss from 640 to 1472 bytes, no fragmentation.
- Some hosts still have a route `mtu lock 680`, so check `ip route get <peer>` first.

## Packet-rate cap

- Kharej → Iran delivers at most about 50–55k ICMP packets/s, shared by every ICMP type. That is about 33 MB/s at a 640 B payload.
- Past about 45k pps a queue builds (p99 one-way delay +300 ms) and loss rises.
- With 1400 B payloads the same path gave 27.5 MB/s down and 26 MB/s up, with 0.3–0.8 % retransmission (3–5 % at 640 B). The per-packet limit appears to bind, not bytes.

## Volume-triggered reroute

- Twice on 2026-10-12, total ICMP held above ~30 MB/s for a few seconds (34.5 and 41.5 MB/s).
- 5–30 s later, the traffic was rerouted inside Iran (base RTT 40 → 76 ms) for several minutes.
- On the new route, bulk transfers collapse to about 2 MB/s with 50–90 % loss, while light traffic is fine.
- Runs at or below ~27 MB/s never triggered it.
- This looks like a volume-based reaction, not a protocol classifier. Has anyone seen the same on other ASes?

## One-way ICMP blocks

- On some Iran IPs, echo requests from Iran to abroad are dropped (100 % loss), while pings from abroad to the same Iran IP work.
- The block comes and goes from day to day.
- Swapping direction works around it: Kharej sends the requests and Iran answers. Linux on the Iran side then also answers every request itself, so `OutEchoReps` = 2 × `InEchos` in `/proc/net/snmp` unless `icmp_ratemask` or `icmp_echo_ignore_all` is changed.
- Non-echo ICMP types (timestamp 13/14, info 15/16, mask 17/18) pass on the routes we tried.

## CDN

- Iran → Cloudflare → Kharej over `wss`: every variant without ECH failed to connect. The block comes right after the TLS handshake, which points to SNI filtering.
- With ECH it works: 44–48 MB/s down and up to 82 MB/s up with 4 sessions, RTT 109–116 ms (CDN base 86 ms).

## Tooling

The measurements were taken with WatTunnel, an open-source (MIT) tunnel I maintain. Full tables and method are here: https://github.com/JohnWatsoon/WatTunnel/blob/main/docs/TECHNICAL.md#icmp-path-limits-and-pacing

Questions I'd like other data on:
1. Is the ~30 MB/s reroute threshold per destination IP, per source AS, or global?
2. Has anyone else seen the 640 B limit lifted on other routes?

issues.title: Link-password authentication bypass through unvalidated Ed25519 identity keys, also affecting Ironwood routing authentication
issues.body:
This report is generated by AI, I am submitting in a hurry to let you know what is going on.


## Summary

We identified this during an AI-assisted source audit.

A remote peer that can reach a password-protected Yggdrasil listener can supply an Ed25519 public key representing the curve's identity point. The handshake relies on a signature under that peer-supplied key to establish knowledge of the link password. For this degenerate key, signature verification can succeed independently of the signed message, so the password-dependent digest does not provide the intended authentication boundary.

Ironwood also accepts this identity in its routing signature checks. This means its subsequent checks do not compensate for the link-handshake weakness.

This report is based on upstream source inspection. We did not execute a PoC, reproduce an exploit, or validate a live deployment. The supported conclusion is an authentication flaw permitting unauthorized peering and routing-state admission under the conditions below; arbitrary traffic hijacking is not established.

## Source examined

- Yggdrasil `v0.5.14`: [`src/core/version.go`](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/v0.5.14/src/core/version.go#L91), containing the affected link-password verifier.
- Yggdrasil `develop`, inspected on 2026-10-17: the same [handshake logic](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/develop/src/core/version.go#L91), and [connection authorization and handoff](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/develop/src/core/link.go#L589).
- Ironwood `4dfb1af8c1ed`, the dependency selected by the inspected [Yggdrasil develop manifest](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/develop/go.mod): routing behavior described below.
- Go `1.26.0`: the inspected [Ed25519 public-key parsing and verification implementation](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/go1.26.0/src/crypto/internal/fips140/ed25519/ed25519.go#L128), corresponding to the Go baseline declared by that develop manifest.

The release observation concerns the handshake source; the detailed Ironwood trace concerns the pinned develop dependency. We have not established the first affected release, a complete affected-version range, or a fixed release.

## Why the password check fails

In `version_metadata.decode()`, the remote public key is read from the handshake. Its field length is checked, but it is not checked for being an acceptable cryptographic identity.

The receiver then computes a BLAKE2b-512 digest keyed by its configured link password, with the peer's declared public key as input, and calls:

```go
ed25519.Verify(m.publicKey, hash, sig)
```

The critical detail is that the password contributes to the **message being verified**, while the remote peer chooses the **verification key**. There is no separate password-authentication check after this signature succeeds.

In Ed25519, the verification equation is:

```text
[S]B = R + [H(R, A, M)]A
```

Here `A` is the public key, `M` is the signed message, and `R` and `S` are signature components. If `A` is the identity point, the entire message-dependent term vanishes. Message-independent signatures can therefore satisfy the equation even when the sender does not know the password-dependent message.

The inspected Go verifier checks point decoding and scalar encoding, but does not reject this public key. Yggdrasil consequently needs an explicit identity-validity policy at this boundary. This is not a claim that signatures under ordinary, honestly generated Ed25519 public keys can be forged.

## Why Ironwood does not stop the identity

Yggdrasil hands the declared key to Ironwood after its authorization checks. [`network.PacketConn.HandleConn()`](https://github.com/Arceliar/ironwood/blob/4dfb1af8c1ed/network/packetconn.go#L141) rejects a wrong length or the local node's own key, but does not reject small-order points.

## Summary

On Debian package upgrades, `postinst` backs up the existing configuration under `/var/backups`. Older configurations can be mode 0644, so a plain copy leaves the backup containing the private key readable by other users. issues.title: core: bound ws/wss/socks handshakes with a dial timeout
issues.body:
## Summary

Only the plain TCP dial is bounded (5 s). After the TCP connection succeeds:

- the WebSocket HTTP upgrade has **no deadline**;
- the WSS TLS handshake has **no deadline** (the default `TLSHandshakeTimeout` of 10 s does not apply because the transport is built by hand);
- the SOCKS negotiation has **no deadline**.

A peer — or a middlebox — that accepts the TCP connection but never completes the handshake therefore holds the dial open until the peer is removed entirely, wasting the whole backoff cycle on a dead attempt.

## Fix

Introduce a shared `wsDialTimeout` (15 s, a variable so tests can shorten it) and apply it to each stage:

- `http.Client.Timeout` for the ws/wss upgrade (the websocket library turns it into a deadline for the handshake only, so the upgraded connection is not affected);
- `TLSHandshakeTimeout` for the WSS TLS handshake, which also bounds a dial the transport may finish in the background after the request is cancelled;
- a context-bounded SOCKS negotiation via `DialContext` when the proxy supports it (the `x/net` SOCKS5 dialer does).

Files: `src/core/link_ws.go`, `src/core/link_wss.go`, `src/core/link_socks.go`.

## Tests

- `TestWSDialTimeout`, `TestWSSDialTimeout`, `TestSOCKSDialTimeout`: a server accepts TCP and never answers; each dial must be abandoned at the timeout (1 s in the tests). Without the change all three fail.
- `TestWSDialTimeoutSparesUpgradedConn`: an upgraded ws/wss connection keeps working after the timeout has passed.
- The shared test logger now sets its call depth up front: `gologme/log` sets it lazily on first output, which the race detector flags when several goroutines log for the first time at once.

`go test ./...` passes, and the new tests pass under `-race`.

Closing the per-dial transport, so that cancelled dials do not leave sockets behind, is a separate follow-up: #1383.

comments.body:
Thanks for following up on this.

For the record, we found this first, with the help of AI tooling; the issue was opened by @peigongdsd. We'd like to keep working on this together with you privately from here.

The 64-byte value asked for is the signature `R || S`:

    A   = 0100...00   (declared public key, ed25519 identity element)
    R   = 0100...00
    S   = 0000...00
    sig = R || S = 0100...00 || 0000...00   (64 bytes)

It is independent of the hashed password: verification checks `[S]*B == R + [k]*A` with `k = H(R || A || M)`. When the declared public key is the identity element `O`, `[k]*O = O` for every `k`, so the equation reduces to `[S]*B == R`. With `S = 0, R = O` this holds for any `M`, and the password only ever enters through `k`, which multiplies `A = O`. Hence the same constant signature verifies for any password.

`R` is not arbitrary: it must equal `[S]*B`; `S` may be any canonical scalar. This is the `S = 0` case.

The class is the whole small-order subgroup rather than just `O` (order-2/4/8 keys also verify certain signatures), so the fix should reject small-order keys, and ideally use strict verification (reject small-order `A`, small-order `R`, non-canonical `S`) at every verification site: the link handshake, ironwood's per-message peer auth, and the encrypted/session handshake.

We have a minimal, self-contained PoC (a single Go file using the real `crypto/ed25519`, no network) that reproduces this and shows the acceptance rates per order. We also confirmed the full impact end to end: using a modified Yggdrasil **Windows client** connecting to an unmodified, normal Yggdrasil node, we joined a password-protected network with no password and no private key. The node we joined is our own, but its password is locked away and we could not have retrieved it. The only copy is inside an encrypted ZIP. The node accepted us as a peer and we loaded an HTTP page served on that network.

Since this is an unfixed authentication bypass, we would rather not post exploit details publicly yet, and we would be glad to go through whatever private channel you prefer, such as GitHub private vulnerability reporting, email, or Matrix. Please let us know how you would like to proceed, and we can share the full PoC, the end-to-end details and a regression test privately so we can coordinate a fix and disclosure together.

If it does qualify, would it be possible to get a CVE assigned for this?

We received a third-party account describing the interaction beyond the initial handshake. The following analysis is based on that account, the supplied screenshot, and upstream source inspection. **Taken as accurately reported, the exchange achieved unauthorized admission as a direct Ironwood peer and sustained participation in its routing protocol.** The attacker reached the processing path that creates peer state, exchanges routing messages, and issues parent authorizations, despite not knowing the link password. | The node sent a SigReq at approximately 0.04 seconds; the client returned a forged SigRes. | The connection had entered Ironwood's peer protocol. |
| At approximately 1.25 seconds, the client received a SigRes containing request fields, a peer port, and a purported node signature. | The node reportedly processed the client's request and supplied the parent authorization used by the routing protocol. |

issues.title: HTTP outbound: Fix hang on server-first protocols
issues.body:
The HTTP outbound waits for the first client payload before it sends CONNECT. With protocols where the server talks first (FTP, SMTP, MySQL, or SSH clients that wait for the server banner, which is probably what #3459 ran into with XShell/MobaXterm) the client waits for the greeting and Xray waits for the client, so the connection hangs until one side gives up.

- Read the first payload with a 500 ms timeout, like the VLESS outbound does since #1425, so a server greeting gets through after at most 500 ms.
- After the `200`, keep tunneled bytes that `bufio` already read together with the response instead of dropping them.

v2fly has the same two changes: v2fly/v2ray-core#1517 and the `Buffered()` drain in its `connectHTTP1`.

Tests (both fail on main):
- `TestHTTPOutboundServerFirst` in `testing/scenarios`: dokodemo → HTTP outbound → HTTP inbound → a server that sends first.
- `TestHTTP1TunnelKeepsDataReadWithResponse` in `proxy/http`: the proxy writes the `200` and the greeting in one write.

Also tried with real binaries: FTP to vsftpd 3.0.5 through the HTTP outbound, via Xray's HTTP inbound, squid 6.13 and Caddy 2.11.7 forward_proxy, and from a SOCKS inbound with sniffing, times out on main and works with this change. Plain HTTP latency and throughput are unchanged.

issues.title: XDRIVE transport: Support two-step template operations (hrefPath)
issues.body:
### Why

Some storage APIs never take or return file content in the API call itself. The Yandex Disk REST API is one:
`GET /v1/disk/resources/upload?path=…` and `GET /v1/disk/resources/download?path=…` answer with JSON
`{"href": "<presigned URL>"}`, and the content goes to or comes from that URL. Today a template op is a single
request, so the template service cannot store segments on Yandex Disk through REST. The only one-request
alternative, WebDAV, is refused on free Disk accounts ("WebDAV is not available for the free tariff.", HTTP 402,
checked 2026-10-16 on a free and on a Yandex Plus account).

### What

`opTemplate` gets two optional fields:

- `hrefPath` — a JSON path (same syntax as `tokenPath`) in the first answer that holds the URL of a second request;
- `hrefMethod` — the method of that request, `GET` by default.

With `hrefPath` set, the first request is sent without the payload, then the href is called with the payload and its
answer is what Put/Get/List/Delete see. The href is called as given — no `{…}` substitution, no auth, no template
headers — so credentials never reach the content host. A non-2xx first answer is returned unchanged, so a 404 from
`/download` still reads as a missing object. Retries and the concurrency limit apply to both requests.
Templates without `hrefPath` behave exactly as before.

### Example: Yandex Disk REST

```json
"template": {
  "flatten": true,
  "auth": {"type": "static", "header": {"Authorization": "OAuth {secret0}"}},
  "put":    {"url": "https://cloud-api.yandex.net/v1/disk/resources/upload?path=disk:/{folder}/{name}&overwrite=true",
             "hrefPath": "href", "hrefMethod": "PUT"},
  "get":    {"url": "https://cloud-api.yandex.net/v1/disk/resources/download?path=disk:/{folder}/{name}",
             "hrefPath": "href"},
  "delete": {"method": "DELETE",
             "url": "https://cloud-api.yandex.net/v1/disk/resources?path=disk:/{folder}/{name}&permanently=true"},
  "list":   {"url": "https://cloud-api.yandex.net/v1/disk/resources?path=disk:/{folder}&limit=10000&fields=_embedded.items.name",
             "namesRegex": "\"name\":\"([^\"]+)\""},
  "retry":  {"status": [423, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]}
}
```

With an `app:/` path and an OAuth app limited to `cloud_api:disk.app_folder`, the shared secret can only touch the
app folder, not the whole Disk.

### Tests

- `TestTemplateTwoStep`: put/get through a fake REST-style store, 404 → `errNotFound`, no credentials sent to the href.
- `TestTemplateTwoStepTransport`: a full client/server stream over the two-step store.
- Both fail without the change; `go test ./transport/internet/xdrive/` passes.

Live (free Yandex Disk account, client and server on one macOS host, VLESS over xdrive, mux on):
first run HTTPS page 13 s cold / 11 s after reconnect, 1 MB download at ~66 KB/s, 300 KB upload at ~15 KB/s,
no errors, segments cleaned up (0 objects left). Later runs the same day were slower and flakier
(HTTPS 22–33 s, some requests timing out, 24–34 KB/s), equally with the change on 0888beb and rebased on
3834e50, so that is Yandex-side variance, not the patch. Every op checked on its own against Yandex after the
rebase: put/list/get/404/delete all fine.

Docs: `hrefPath` / `hrefMethod` would need a line in the XDRIVE template section of Xray-docs-next.

issues.title: sockopt.interface: when the interface does not exist, the dial silently goes unbound (can loop back into TUN)
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

If an outbound has `streamSettings.sockopt.interface` set and that interface does not exist at dial time, Xray does not fail the dial. It logs `failed to apply socket options > failed to get interface ...` at **Info** level and opens the connection without any binding, so it follows the system routing table.

`transport/internet/system_dialer.go` (v26.10.10, lines 134-139; same in v26.9.9) only logs the error returned by `applyOutboundSocketOptions` and goes on to `dialer.DialContext`. The UDP path does the same (lines 77-81). The error itself comes from `net.InterfaceByName` in `transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go:136-140`. From reading the source, Linux takes the same path (the error is logged, not returned); I tested macOS only.

Why this matters. A typical full-tunnel setup on a desktop routes everything into a TUN interface handled by Xray (default route split as 0.0.0.0/1 + 128.0.0.0/1 into the TUN), and binds outbounds with `sockopt.interface` so that their own sockets do not enter the TUN again. If the bound interface goes away, the fallback sends the outbound's sockets into the TUN, Xray routes them to the same outbound, and the connection loops.

We hit this loop in practice on macOS. A separate OpenVPN client provided a corporate network through its own utun interface, and the corporate subnet was routed to a freedom outbound so that it would follow that VPN's route. At night the OpenVPN client lost its connection and its utun interface was removed. From then on, every connection to the corporate subnet (including DNS queries to the corporate DNS server) entered the TUN, came back to the same outbound and entered the TUN again. When we looked, there were about 8,000 looped connections, all 16,384 ephemeral ports were in use, and other processes on the host got `EADDRNOTAVAIL` (`Can't assign requested address`) on connect until the loop was broken by restarting Xray.

In that incident the outbound had no `sockopt.interface` at all, so the loop itself is a config problem. The obvious fix is to bind the outbound to the other VPN's interface (`"interface": "utunN"`), so that it can never fall into the TUN. That does not work because of this issue: once the interface disappears, the binding is skipped and the loop is back. The only visible sign is an Info-level log line, which is hidden at the usual `warning` level.

Expected: if the interface named in `sockopt.interface` cannot be found, the dial fails (fail closed), as a bound socket does when its interface has no route. At the very least the error should be logged as a warning. A silent fallback to the routing table defeats the purpose of binding: it can send traffic into a tunnel (loop) or past it (leak).

### Reproduction Method

No server and no TUN are needed. Run Xray with the config below (interface `utun99` does not exist) and send a request through the SOCKS inbound:

```
curl --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 http://example.com/
```

Result: HTTP 200. The log shows that the interface was not found and the connection was opened anyway; its local endpoint is the address of whatever interface the routing table chose (on our machine, the address of a TUN interface that held the default route).

For comparison, with `"interface": "en0"` the same request goes out through en0 (local endpoint is en0's address) and no error is logged.

Expected result: the connection through the outbound bound

issues.title: XHTTP over HTTP/2: reducing per-stream memory
issues.body:
XHTTP over HTTP/2 uses noticeably more memory than RAW on both ends. This shows up most on memory-limited clients (#5944, #6268).

Previous discussions:

- #6268: the client allocates a per-stream upload scratch buffer of `min(peer SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE, 512 KiB)` and holds it for the whole life of the stream, although a single body read in Xray never returns more than 8 KiB. With REALITY/TLS straight to an Xray server the peer advertises 1 MiB, so every idle stream on a reused xmux connection holds 512 KiB.
- golang/go#79831: proposal to lower that cap to 32 KiB in Go. Open since June with no decision.
- #6663: advertising 16 KiB from the Xray server. Not planned, because a CDN in front of the server advertises its own value.

There are two separate causes:

1. **Idle streams.** The 512 KiB scratch buffer described above.
2. **Slow readers.** Go's HTTP/2 flow-control windows are fixed: 1 MiB per stream on the server, 4 MiB on the client. When the reader is slower than the link (a video player with a full buffer, a relay whose next hop is slower, a slow upload target), the peer fills the whole window and the data sits unread in process memory. While the reader keeps up there is no difference. Kernel TCP avoids this with receive-buffer autotuning. Go's HTTP/2 has nothing like it: golang/go#63520 only proposes static window settings, and a small static window caps throughput on high-BDP paths.

### Idle streams: options until Go changes

- Patch `frameScratchBufferLen` (512 KiB → 32 KiB) in GOROOT and in vendored x/net in the release workflow. This is quick, but it only reaches official release binaries; mobile apps and distributions that build from source do not get it.
- Cap the peer's `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE` at 16 KiB inside Xray before `net/http` reads it (part of the proposal below). This works for every build and behind any CDN.

### Proposal

A frame-level shim between the TLS/REALITY conn and `net/http` that manages HTTP/2 flow control on its own side of the connection. It needs no x/net fork, no toolchain patch and no config fields.

- **Frame size:** the peer's `SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE` is rewritten to 16 KiB in both directions. On the client this caps the scratch buffer at 16 KiB whatever the server or a CDN advertises, which addresses the concern in #6663. On the server it does the same for stock clients.
- **Windows:** each stream starts at the protocol default of 64 KiB. The window grows to twice what the reader consumed per RTT (RTT measured by PING, the same idea as gRPC-Go's BDP estimator) and shrinks by a quarter at a time once the reader stays well below it. It is bounded on both sides: never above what stock Go would grant, and never below 64 KiB or twice the current consumption per RTT.
- **Roles:** the server governs uploads and downloads; the client governs downloads only. It works with unmodified official Xray and mihomo peers. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/3 are not touched. It can be disabled with `XRAY_XHTTP_FLOW=off`.

### Measurements

Idle upload streams: 40 streams on a reused connection, heap of both ends in one process.

| server | client | heap per stream |
|---|---|---|
| stock | stock | ~555 KiB |
| stock (same as behind a CDN) | shim | ~65 KiB |
| shim | stock | ~67 KiB |

Slow readers: 100 Mbit/s, 50 ms RTT, 30 sessions, REALITY.

| scenario | stock | shim |
|---|---|---|
| client, app reads downloads slowly | 146 MB | 31–65 MB |
| server, receiver of uploads is slow | 70 MB | 20 MB |
| fast then slow stream, unread data per stream | 4.2 MB | 0.17 MB |
| latency behind a bulk transfer | ~1.1 s | ~0.1 s |

Steady-state throughput is unchanged. The cost is a slower ramp for new streams: 5-second transfers are 3% slower at 30 ms RTT, 13% at 80 ms and 30% at 150 ms.

Tested with REALITY and TLS × stream-one, stream-up and packet-up against official Xray and mihomo clients, plus model, fuzz and `-race` tests and soak runs, with no leaks, stalls or data corruption.

### Description

> 简述：v26.9.8 起使用 Go 1.27 构建，x/net http2.Transport 改为包装 net/http.Transport。当 TLS 握手被阻断而挂起时，每个会话都会新建一条 TCP 连接，XMUX 的 maxConnections 实际失效，连接数和内存随会话数线性增长。使用 `-tags http2legacy` 构建可恢复正常。与 #6644 不同，这里的额外连接与 MaxConcurrentStreams 无关。

Since v26.9.8 Xray is built with Go 1.27 (`fd2ca748`, "go.mod: Specify Go 1.27.x"); the v26.9.9 release binary reports `go1.27.1`, and the release workflow builds without extra tags. With Go 1.27, `golang.org/x/net` (v0.58.0 in v26.9.9, v0.59.0 on main) compiles `http2/transport_wrap.go`:

```go
//go:build go1.27 && !http2legacy
// Transport wrapping a net/http.Transport.
```

In this mode `http2.Transport.RoundTrip` is delegated to an internal `net/http.Transport` instead of x/net's own `clientConnPool`. The old pool deduplicated in-flight dials per address (`p.dialing[addr]`), so an XMUX client whose handshake hangs held exactly one socket and all further requests waited on it. The new path does not: while no HTTP/2 connection to the host is established yet, every waiting request dials its own TCP connection.

Normally this is invisible — the first handshake completes in one RTT and everything is multiplexed afterwards. But when handshakes hang (e.g. a middlebox blackholes the flow after the ClientHello — the TSPU scenario from #6376), **every proxied session gets its own TCP connection**. `xmux.maxConnections` still limits the number of XMUX clients (the debug log below shows two `XMUX: creating xmuxClient` lines and no removals), but not the dials underneath them.

Consequences:

- `maxConnections: 2`/`3`, introduced as the anti-TSPU default (`18e28390`, #6376), no longer keeps the client under the ~4-connection limit — it opens hundreds or thousands of connections and keeps re-triggering the ban;
- memory grows linearly with hung sessions; in a memory-limited container the process is OOM-killed, taking every other (healthy) outbound down with it.

**Affected:** v26.9.8, v26.9.9 and main (`d562d894`) — all Go 1.27 + x/net ≥ v0.58.0. v26.7.28 and earlier are built with Go 1.26 and use the legacy transport. Tested: XHTTP `stream-one` over TLS (h2). I did not test `packet-up`/`stream-up` or h3.

**Field observation.** Linux client in an LXC container with a memory limit, VLESS + XHTTP `stream-one` + TLS, `maxConnections: 2` (effective config verified with `xray run -dump`, no `extra`). During a TSPU episode against one server (pcap on the router WAN):

- up to **2348** simultaneously open client sockets to that server; bursts of 26 SYNs within 90 ms;
- 1258 of 1261 new connections: SYN/SYN-ACK OK, the ClientHello is never ACKed, retransmitted for minutes;
- the process was OOM-killed twice, 193 s apart (`Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process ... (xray) ... anon-rss:218772kB`); the healthy HTTP/2 connections of the other outbounds were reset along with it.

Another outbound (different server) in the same process was unaffected — its handshakes complete, so the first HTTP/2 connection is established and everything multiplexes.

issues.title: [Feature Request] XDRIVE: Add configurable object naming for storage backends
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

XDRIVE uses predictable object naming patterns containing session IDs and protocol-specific markers such as `seg` and `end`.

These patterns make XDRIVE activity easily identifiable by cloud storage providers, even when the content itself is encrypted.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add configurable object naming to `xdriveSettings`, allowing object keys to be fully obfuscated instead of exposing XDRIVE's internal naming conventions.

For example (proposed configuration):

```json
"xdriveSettings": {
  "service": "template",
  "objectNaming": {
    "mode": "opaque",
    "secret": "<shared-secret>",
    "encoding": "base64url"
  }
}
```

The naming mechanism should:

- Hide session IDs, `seg`/`end` markers, and other recognizable naming patterns.
- Generate deterministic, reversible opaque names so both endpoints can identify the same objects.
- Preserve existing naming behavior when the option is disabled.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

Maintaining a custom Xray-core fork or using an external storage proxy to rewrite object keys.

### Additional context

This is especially relevant for S3-compatible storage providers using the XDRIVE `template` backend, where object keys are visible to the storage provider.

## Summary

Expose the inbound tags with live authenticated dispatcher links for each online user through `StatsService.GetUsersStats`. This is a draft for discussion of the additive stats API and its consumer; no merge is requested yet.

## Motivation

An account may be used by multiple devices on different inbounds simultaneously. A flat online-user list, inbound byte counters, or a common source IP cannot reliably identify that account's active profiles, especially behind NAT. The companion 3x-ui change displays the exact live profile set, including across nodes.

## Changes

- Track `(authenticated email, inbound tag)` online maps alongside the existing aggregate user map in both dispatcher link paths.
- Reuse the existing context cancellation and OnlineMap reference-counting lifetime. Multiple links from one source IP do not go offline until the last one closes.
- Add `UserStat.inbound_tags` (field 4) and `GetUsersStatsResponse.inbound_tracking` (field 2). The capability distinguishes an older core from a supported empty snapshot; names/field choices are open for review while this is a draft.

- Return deterministically sorted users/tags and cover same-IP isolation, concurrent inbounds, disconnects, namespace parsing, and unchanged byte counters in regression tests.

The feature tracks live authenticated dispatcher links, not a profile merely selected in an app before a connection opens. It does not log destinations, add connection-history storage, or introduce panel-specific configuration/ports.

issues.title: Finalmask: Add the `lua` mask (noise's `script` moves there)
issues.body:
#7174 bolted a second Lua mask onto header-custom, which was the wrong way around. One `lua` mask covers all of it now: it is both a `tcpMasks` and a `udpMasks` entry, and the script decides what it does by the hooks it defines.

-- `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)`, TCP: a free handshake before any traffic, with `stream:Write`, `stream:Read` and `stream:Sleep`. Return a string or an error and the connection is dropped
-- `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` and `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)`, UDP: prefix every packet with a header, and strip it on the other side by returning its length, or `nil` to drop the packet
-- `HandleNoise(plan, address, role)` is the old noise hook, so `noise`'s `script` is gone (it has not been in a release yet)
-- `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends
-- a hook the script does not define is not wrapped at all: a noise only script leaves TCP connections alone and never touches a packet
-- the module is `xray.finalmask` now, with `Random` and `RandomBetween`

```json
{
    "udpMasks": [{"type": "lua", "settings": {"script": "mask.lua", "reset": "30-60"}}]
}
```

Per call it takes at most 64 noise packets and 65535 bytes of noise, 1024 bytes of header, and 65535 bytes each way in a handshake. A packet hook gets 1s, a handshake 30s. A UDP header is one Lua call per packet, the benchmarks in the package cover its cost.

The static lists can follow later, the same script can already do what they do.

issues.title: [Proposal] Plugin System based on WASM (wazero) for Hot-Patching Protocols & Logic on Mobile
issues.body:
Mobile clients (especially iOS) suffer from long App Store review cycles. When a critical bug is found in the core, or when GFW introduces new active probing that requires immediate protocol adjustments, users are left without connection for weeks until a new binary is reviewed and released.

Currently, Xray is monolithic. We cannot update internal logic without replacing the binary. On iOS, dynamic linking of native binaries is strictly forbidden by the OS sandbox.

I propose integrating a pure Go WebAssembly runtime, such as [wazero](https://github.com/wazero/wazero), into Xray-core.

The goal is to define a set of interfaces (hooks) for:
1. Protocol Handlers / Transports (Dialers & Listeners)
2. Obfuscation Logic (Packet manipulation)
3. Routing Rules

Xray should be able to load external `.wasm` modules at runtime (fetched from a remote URL or local storage).

**How it solves the problem:**
1. **Compliance:** WASM is interpreted code, which is allowed by Apple's App Store guidelines (unlike native dlopen).
2. **Hot-Fixes:** Developers can compile a fix (written in Go/Rust/TinyGo) to WASM and push it to clients immediately via a config update.
3. **Flexibility:** We can patch specific logic flaws (for example, the recent problem #5230) without waiting for a full app release.

**Alternatives considered**
- **Starlark/Lua scripting:** Good for routing, but too slow for heavy packet processing/crypto hooks.
- **Go Plugins:** Not supported on mobile architectures and incompatible with iOS security policies.

This architecture would make Xray significantly more resilient against censorship events, allowing the community to deploy countermeasures instantly to millions of mobile users.

issues.title: XHTTP stream-up behind an HTTP/1.1 Nginx upstream truncates uploads
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

Large uploads through XHTTP `stream-up` fail for me when Nginx forwards the XHTTP requests to Xray over HTTP/1.1. Curl reports that it sent the whole body, but the destination receives only part of it, or the connection fails before the destination can parse the request.

I reduced this to a local Docker setup with a synthetic JSON body. There is no CDN, external API, authentication header, or TLS in the minimal reproduction.

Tested versions:
- Xray main, commit `0f3d884786f9ec73d3be8899cb6b9e1e6dd3c41e`.
- Binary: `Xray 26.10.10 Custom (go1.27.1 linux/amd64)`.
- Nginx image: `nginx:1.28-alpine`.
- Curl image: `curlimages/curl:8.12.1`.
- I also reproduced the HTTP/1.1 problem on Xray v26.3.27 / Go 1.26.1.

The test body is 1,385,909 bytes. In the minimal run shown in the logs, the destination received **7,999 bytes followed by EOF**, while curl reported the full upload and got HTTP 503 after about 5 ms. The received length varies between runs. I expected the destination to receive the complete body and return HTTP 200.

Two changes make the same test pass:
- Set `scStreamUpServerSecs: -1` on the XHTTP **server inbound**. This disables the POST response keepalive, so it has an idle-timeout trade-off.
- Leave response keepalive enabled, but change Nginx's backend hop to HTTP/2 using `grpc_pass`. Xray still uses XHTTP `stream-up`, not the gRPC transport.

On the main build, the original HTTP/1.1 setup delivered 0/10 bodies intact. Disabling response keepalive passed 4/4. HTTP/2 upstream passed 6/6 fast uploads and another 2/2 uploads limited to 32 KiB/s, lasting about 42 seconds each. For those slow tests I set the server response padding interval to one second. The HTTP/2 tests covered HTTP forwarding and HTTPS CONNECT with synthetic bodies. The release v26.3.27 also passed 4/4 fast HTTP/2-upstream tests. Direct XHTTP without Nginx passed both control probes.

I suspect the early POST response interacts with Go's HTTP/1 request-body handling. The server log contains `http: invalid Read on closed Body`. The stream-up handler reads the POST body while writing response padding, without enabling HTTP/1 full duplex. Nginx removes the client's `Connection: close` header in this setup, so the backend is taking a different HTTP/1 response path from the direct connection.

This is not a confirmed complete explanation: I also tested an experimental `EnableFullDuplex` change, and it only passed 4/10 probes; the others stalled after receiving a body prefix. On the v26.3.27 baseline, a full capture showed that Nginx received and forwarded identical decoded POST bodies, yet bytes were missing at the destination. So I do not think the evidence points to Nginx simply dropping bytes from the upload.

Relevant handler: https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/0f3d884786f9ec73d3be8899cb6b9e1e6dd3c41e/transport/internet/splithttp/hub.go#L198-L242

Could the concurrent POST body reads and response keepalive writes be handled differently for HTTP/1 upstreams?

### Reproduction Method

Attach `public-repro.tar.gz` from this report. It contains the Dockerfile, Compose file, exact combined Xray config, Nginx config, and a small Python receiver. It generates its own synthetic body; no private request or credentials are needed.

The topology is:

```text
curl -> Xray HTTP inbound :8080
     -> VLESS / XHTTP stream-up outbound
     -> Nginx :80
     -> Xray VLESS / XHTTP inbound :144

issues.title: Finalmask header-custom: Support Lua `script` as well
issues.body:
builds on the lua engine from #6823 and the noise hook from #7124, docs will follow once #909 is merged

-- `header-custom` takes a `script`, which can't be set together with `clients`, `servers`, `errors` or the udp `client`, `server`. the script's path resolves like the other lua ones and `infra` only compiles it, so a typo is caught at startup while the pool is created the first time a layer needs a header
-- tcp: `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)` runs the whole handshake, `stream:Write(bytes)`, `stream:Read(size)` and `stream:Sleep(ms)`. `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends like the static config does. returning an error fails the connection, which is what `header auth failed` already does, and a server can `stream:Write` a fake answer before it returns, the way the static `errors` sequences work
-- udp: `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` builds the prefix with `header:Add(bytes)` and `header:AddRandom(size)`, `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)` returns how many bytes to strip, or nil to drop the packet, and reads it through `packet:Len()`, `packet:Byte(at)`, `packet:Match(at, bytes)` and `packet:Slice(from, to)`
-- no new module: the engine registers the public `RegisterLua` of `xray.finalmask.noise`, so a header script gets `Random` and `RandomBetween` from there, plus `xray.log`

everything a static header does can be written in lua: fixed bytes, `rand`, `randRange` byte by byte, the delays, the server's error answer, and `capture`/`reuse` become plain locals because a handshake happens in one call. `"mode": "standalone"` still refuses a script, the udp handshake there would want its own hook

no LTable on either path, one stream, one builder and one packet view per instance, reused, and the numbers are checked: a handshake takes at most 65535 bytes in and 65535 out, a udp header at most 1024, and every size, index and delay is validated before it is converted so a huge float or a nan can't slip through. a shared config can't make the hooks allocate without bound

the tcp hook holds its pooled instance for the handshake, since `stream:Read` waits for the peer. that is the half duplex part of @Meo597's idea, the payload never goes through lua, so this needs no event framework. if you'd rather wait for one, say so and i'll park the tcp half

`BenchmarkLuaHeader` is in the package: per packet a udp header costs about ten times the static one, 424 bytes in eight allocations against 24 in three, so the static lists stay the better choice at high packet rates. the tcp hook runs once per connection

timeouts: 30s for a handshake because it waits for the peer, 1s per udp packet, and the instance init stays 120s

issues.title: Proposal: user-configurable traffic shaping profiles for XMC / FinalMask (follow-up to #6487)
issues.body:
The #6487 summary ends with:

> This intentionally does not emit version-specific Play or Chunk Data packets. **User-configurable traffic shaping is deferred to a follow-up PR.**

In the merge discussion @RPRX also noted that custom traffic-shape configuration would be added later as an incremental feature (流量形状自定义配置下次再补吧，毕竟是增量功能).

This issue proposes a concrete design for that follow-up and asks for design agreement before any implementation (a draft PR would follow if the direction is acceptable). If the original XMC author already has shaping work in flight, happy to stand down and review/help instead.

## Problem

The current XMC shaping is a built-in model of one fixed target (uncompressed Minecraft 26.1.2 login/join). Two practical limits:

- Built-in models decay when the camouflage target's traffic shape evolves; updating them requires core releases.
- Different deployments may need different camouflage targets, but today the XMC shape is a compiled-in preset and is not configurable (other masks, e.g. fragment #6334 or header-custom #5920, already take declarative config).

The knobs that exist today are scattered across features and do not compose with XMC's directional shaping: freedom fragment `maxSplit` (#4998), XHTTP upload pacing (`minUploadInterval`, #3592) and its padding mechanism (#3643), fragment `lengths`/`delays` (#6334), and the programmable `header-custom` templates (#5920).

## Proposal

Make the XMC shaping data-driven: a declarative profile loaded from config, interpreted by a small engine in `finalmask` — no policy logic in core.

Sketch:

```jsonc
{
  "schema": "xray.shape@1",
  "name": "xmc-default",
  "version": 1,
  "phases": {
    "login": {
      "c2s": { "lenDist": [ /* sampled length histogram */ ] },
      "s2c": { "lenDist": [ /* ... */ ] },
      "keepAlive": { "iatMs": 1000, "jitterMs": 100 }
    }
    // phase transitions follow the existing protocol state machine
  }
}
```

Runtime invariants (deliberately conservative):

- Padding only ever increases record length; shortening is fragmentation, which stays a separate mask.
- Zero added latency for real data: the profile only rate-limits sends (`iatMs` as "not faster than") and fills pauses with dummies. Delay-based scheduling is explicitly out of scope here.
- The turn schedule stays alternating-direction (client first), exactly like the merged XMC padding schedule; a profile only controls lengths and cadence, never the message flow.
- `shape` composes with the other configured masks rather than replacing them; the chain order stays whatever the `finalmask.tcp` array says (noise in particular remains a standalone pre-data layer).
- Fail-closed: schema/`version` mismatch between endpoints aborts the connection.
- Length values the server must reproduce are carried in-band, inside the encrypted channel.

## What this is not

- Not a new protocol and not a wire-format change.
- Not ML in core: profiles are produced offline elsewhere; core only interprets a table. A separate profile repository and geodata-style distribution can come later — out of scope here.
- Not delay/jitter scheduling (possible follow-up after measurements).

## Questions

1. Config placement: a profile embedded in `streamSettings` (per inbound/outbound), or a named registry referenced by id?
2. Are the invariants above (especially zero-delay + padding-only) the intended direction for the follow-up, or was something broader planned?
3. If the direction is agreed, would a draft PR with a single built-in preset (reproducing today's XMC 26.1.2 shape as a profile), tests, and the still missing XMC config docs be the right first step?

Prior art for profile-driven shaping engines: Maybenot (Karlstad University, arXiv:2304.09510) — a padding engine driven by parameterized state machines; the offline-profile / online-interpreter split here follows the same reasoning at the proxy layer.

Refs: #6487 #6210 #4998 #3592 #3643 #6334 #5920

When there is a domain (sniffing or fakedns), freedom already handles it: with `AsIs`, Go's dialer falls back to IPv4, and with `UseIP`/`ForceIP` in `sockopt.domainStrategy`, Xray's happy eyeballs does, since the IPv6 attempt now fails at once when binding fails.

**The real problem is a direct connection to a bare IPv6 address that can't be sniffed**: there is no IPv6 path, so it can't work, and the best we can do is fail it as early as possible so that the app falls back to IPv4. **But the TUN comes before routing: it has already completed the TCP handshake before Xray even decides where the connection goes**, so by the time the direct dial fails, it's too late for the app to notice.

I think the TUN should keep routing IPv6 even if the outbound interface has no IPv6. Suppose a program sends data to an IPv6 address: we want it to go through our proxy server, which has IPv6, not to bypass Xray or fail on our device. Xray carries it inside its connection to the server, which can be plain IPv4, and the server reaches the IPv6 address on its side. comments.body:
Ai said this:

on the hook bitmask. a shared mask gives every state one answer and costs an atomic load per call, and more to the point it is what lets a mask decide not to wrap a connection at all when its hook is missing, which a live lookup cannot undo after the fact. clearing bits and never setting them makes dynamic registration impossible by construction instead of by convention, which is the property you asked for. a live lookup would always match the state that is about to run and would leave room for re-registration, but four `GetGlobal` lookups are about 4% of one header hook call on a packet, and states would then start behaving differently from one another, which is harder to reason about than one shared answer. the real cost of probing once is a script that defines a hook conditionally, by time or by chance, which can be probed wrong, so the docs should say hooks are defined at the top level, and logging the hooks found at init would make a typo visible instead of silent.

on the declaration style. globals need no core change, they are the shape dns and router already ship, and there is nothing for the engine to inject; the cost is that a mistake is silent, `HandleHeaderWirte` simply means no hook and the mask passes traffic through instead of failing. a returned table is explicit and discoverable, a natural place for metadata later, and it lets a hook be a closure instead of a global, but it needs `PCall(0, 1)` plus per state storage in core, and the engine would then want to inject `unregister`, which dns and router can never honour, so that debt lands on the two that cannot unload. a register call is the only one of the three that allows registration inside a closure or a branch, which is exactly what several state instances cannot support, so ruling it out is right. globals now, with a standalone unload function later if one is ever needed, leaves the least behind.

on permission levels. gating early costs little and spares you reviewing the same risk twice; the counter risk is freezing the wrong split while nothing uses it yet. the surface here is narrow: no filesystem, no new sockets, only the connection the mask was handed, with caps on bytes and packets and a timeout per hook. the one api that can hold a pooled state is `stream:Sleep`, and a blocking api has to respect the state context or the timeout is decoration and a level buys nothing. a split that should survive contact is everything that only produces bytes, the noise plan, the header builder and the packet view, at the lowest level, with raw stream read and write plus sleep one level above, so that `register` simply does not install the stream object below that level and no call site has to change when signing comes back.

comments.issue_title: Finalmask: Add the `lua` mask (noise's `script` moves there)
comments.body:
bitmask is in. the engine keeps an `atomic.Uint32`, the first state fills it and `validate` rejects a script with no hook at all. a hook a script drops is cleared for the whole engine so every other state short circuits it too, and bits only ever get cleared, never set, so nothing can register one later even by accident. the wrap decision stays where it was: a mask whose hook the script doesn't define returns the raw conn and isn't wrapped at all, the bit only decides whether an already wrapped conn still goes into Lua. two tests for it, one drops `HandleHeaderWrite` after the first packet and the rest go out bare, one drops `HandleNoise` and a new destination gets no noise either.

agreed on keeping the globals, and the injected `unregister` is the right reason. two more in favour: `NewState` runs the chunk with `L.PCall(0, 0, nil)`, so whatever a script returns is dropped today and the table would need a core change first, and `HandleDNSQuery`/`HandleRoute` are already released (#6823 merged at 09:01 on the 10th, v26.10.10 tagged at 09:21 the same day), so globals are the released convention and not only the current one. starting from zero i'd have said the table, since that's what pooled plugin hosts tend to do (kong plugins end with `return Handler`, plain lua modules `return M`), but with those two released and unable to unload, a standalone function later beats a table field they'd never implement.

VLESS TCP + REALITY + Vision stopped passing traffic when using `www.microsoft.com:443` as the REALITY target. The server accepted connections, but websites would not load through the VPN.

Packet capture showed that port 443 was reachable and the TCP handshake completed. The client then sent approximately 1.9 KB of initial data. The server acknowledged it and closed the connection with FIN, without sending any TLS payload. The client kept retrying.

To isolate the failure, we ran a temporary Xray client on the VPS and connected to the existing inbound over loopback. The same failure occurred locally, so neither the home network nor ISP filtering was required to reproduce it. Ordinary TLS connections from the VPS to Microsoft succeeded.

An isolated test server using the same REALITY credentials produced these diagnostic lines:

```text
hs.c.conn == conn: true
Certificate: 8273
hs.c.isHandshakeComplete.Load(): false
handshake did not complete successfully
```

REALITY authentication passed, but processing the target’s response failed. Microsoft returned a **8273-byte Certificate TLS record**, exceeding the **8192-byte limit** in the REALITY implementation used by this version.

This explains why checking port availability and establishing an ordinary TLS connection to the target did not reveal the problem: the failure occurred inside REALITY’s handshake processing.

Connectivity was restored by changing the server target and updating the client SNI consistently:

```text
Server target:      www.nvidia.com:443
Server serverNames: ["www.nvidia.com"]
Client SNI:         www.nvidia.com
```

UUIDs, keys, short IDs, port 443 and `flow=xtls-rprx-vision` were preserved. After the change, HTTPS requests through the production TCP inbound returned HTTP 200 with both `chrome` and `firefox` fingerprints. Connectivity from the previously affected home network was also restored.

Clients need to refresh their subscriptions or update the SNI in manually imported profiles. NVIDIA worked for this deployment; the suitability of a target should be tested for each server.

These results confirm the existing issue on version 26.6.27, not a regression in a release containing the fix. The core was not upgraded during this investigation.

yeah, better to settle it now than refactor it later.

-- 1. the engine probes the four hooks once when it builds the pool and keeps them in a struct, and `validate` errors if a script defines none. the point of caching isn't the lookup, it's that a mask whose hook isn't defined returns the raw conn and never gets wrapped, so TCP keeps `Splice` and a packet doesn't go through anything. four `GetGlobal` lookups cost about 4% of one header hook call on a packet and the cached read about 0.03%, so checking live is affordable too if you want scripts to unload hooks later. but a conn that was never wrapped can't grow a hook back, so unloading needs the engine rebuilt and a reload already does that. a global script that isn't pooled can just call `defined()` live, it's the same function.

-- 2. globals, same as `HandleDNSQuery` and `HandleRoute`. i'd rather keep one convention for every script type than have finalmask declare its hooks differently. if you want explicit declaration (`fm.OnNoise(f)`) this is the moment for all three and i'll do it here first, it also gives you the unloading from 1 and lets a hook be a closure instead of a global.

-- 3. nothing here reaches outside the conn the mask was handed: the script reads and writes that conn during the handshake, builds a header, fills a noise plan, all bounded (65535 bytes each way per handshake, 1024 bytes of header, 64 packets and 65535 bytes of noise per call). the one that can hold a pooled state is `stream:Sleep`, and the hook's timeout cuts it short now instead of parking the state for a minute. for the level, `register` can't see it today and `Program.privileged` is unexported, so tell me which you want, `register func(*glua.LState, Level)` or an exported accessor, and i'll put the stream object behind it.

This adds an opt-in setting that blocks that. It is the last of three PRs, and the other two carry the datapath (merge order below). ## What the user gets A **"Strict split tunneling"** switch, shown on Android only and off by default. It sits under "App-based split tunneling" in the split tunneling drawer on the home screen and in Settings → Connection. The app split tunneling page itself is unchanged. - Description: *Blocks bypasses of the tunneling rules. Strictly prevents apps from using the VPN tunnel directly unless they are allowed to use the VPN. Supports AmneziaWG and WireGuard.* - It is enabled only when app split tunneling is on, the default server's protocol is AmneziaWG (either container) or WireGuard, and the VPN is disconnected. The setting is read when the tunnel starts, like the rest of split tunneling. - Turning it on first shows a question drawer that explains what it does and the Private DNS caveat below. | | | | | |---|---|---|---| | Off by default | Turning it on explains the trade-off | On | Locked while connected | ## How it works - `StrictSplitTunnelGuard` (`android/utils`) decides per connection. It asks `ConnectivityManager.getConnectionOwnerUid` (API 29+) for the owning app and applies include or exclude mode to the app lists. An unresolved owner is denied. Android returns `INVALID_UID` both when no socket matches and when the owner is not covered by this VPN, and an excluded app is exactly the second case. The guard keeps no state: amneziawg-go caches its verdicts per 5-tuple and asks from several threads at once. - `Wireguard.kt` registers the guard with the AmneziaWG backend through `GoBackend.awgSetUidFilter` right before the tunnel is turned on. issues.title: [Android] [Critical] Per-app split tunneling bypass for AmneziaWG 2.0 allows blacklisted apps to see the ip address of the VPN.
issues.body:
**Summary**
It was mentioned in the previous commit but the person responsible for fixing it did it only for XRay so I feel obligated to mention it again. You can get the ip of the VPN server by explicitly going through the tun0 interface. Like this (in Termux).  `curl -s https://ifconfig.me/ip --interface tun0`
That will allow any spyware (which now includes every russian big-tech app) to not only get the fact that you use a VPN but also get the ip address of the server. Then they can log it, and later block it.


**Environment**

- App version: 4.8.14.5
- Android version: 14
- Device: Samsung Galaxy A33 5G
- Protocol used: AmneziaWG 2.0
- Split tunneling: Enabled (Termux excluded from VPN)

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
 1. Install AmneziaVPN and configure a working connection.
 2. Enable Per-app VPN (split tunneling) and exclude Termux (or any test app with INTERNET permission).
 3. Connect to the VPN.
 4. In Termux, run:
```
#Send traffic through the tun0 interface
curl -s https://ifconfig.me/ip --interface tun0
# Observed: VPN exit IP`

```
**Expected behavior**
Applications excluded from VPN routing should not be able to send traffic through the VPN tunnel via a localhost proxy, unless this behavior is explicitly documented and user-controlled. If a local listener is required for internal purposes, access should be restricted to the app's own components.

**Security Impact**
If the proxy accepts unauthenticated connections and forwards traffic through the VPN tunnel:

-  User-configured per-app routing policies can be bypassed by any app with INTERNET permission.

-  Traffic that the user explicitly intended to route directly may leak through the VPN (or vice versa).

-  The presence of an open, unauthenticated localhost proxy may serve as a detectable signal of VPN usage to monitoring applications.

**Operational relevance**
In environments where applications or platforms monitor network behavior for signs of VPN usage, this issue may increase the detectability of VPN use. Because an app excluded from VPN routing can still access the VPN tunnel via localhost, it can both infer that the VPN is active and send probe traffic through the tunnel. This may also aid enumeration of VPN egress IPs and contribute to blocking of VPN endpoints. This consideration is particularly relevant given recent reports of app-level VPN detection guidelines being distributed to IT platforms [1][2].

**Suggested Mitigations**
The same that solved SOCKS5 leak (will be solved if someone merges [this](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/pull/2453) pull request).

-  Require authentication (username/password) for the tun0 interface, if the feature is intended for external use.
-  If there is any alternative way to get the VPN ip address without being in the split-tunneling whitelist - fix it.

I repeat that this vulnerability while not as critical poses a significant threat to the VPN's hosted on private servers which were mostly immune to the direct ip blocking from Russian censors.

issues.title: [Bug] AmneziaWG 2 Docker container has IPv4 forwarding disabled after automatic installation in Proxmox LXC
issues.body:
**Title: [Bug] AmneziaWG 2 Docker container has IPv4 forwarding disabled after automatic installation in Proxmox LXC**

### Environment

- Host: Proxmox VE
- Guest: Debian 13, unprivileged LXC with nesting enabled
- VPN: AmneziaWG 2, installed automatically using the official Amnezia Android app
- Docker: 26.1.5+dfsg1 (installed by Amnezia)
- Also reproduced with preinstalled Docker 29.8.0
- `/dev/net/tun` passed through from Proxmox into LXC
- Container: `amnezia-awg2`

### Problem

The official Android app successfully installs AmneziaWG 2. The client establishes a VPN connection and completes the handshake, but neither internet nor LAN traffic works.

The VPN interface, UDP listener, NAT rules, and firewall rules are present.

The underlying problem is that IPv4 forwarding is disabled **inside the AmneziaWG Docker container**, despite being enabled in the parent LXC.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a fresh Debian 13 unprivileged Proxmox LXC with Docker nesting and TUN passthrough.
2. Install AmneziaWG 2 using the official Android app, allowing it to install Docker.
3. Connect from Android.
4. Observe a successful handshake but no internet or LAN connectivity.
5. Run:

   `docker exec amnezia-awg2 sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward`

   Result: `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0`

6. Enable forwarding:

   `docker exec amnezia-awg2 sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`

7. Internet and LAN connectivity immediately work, without restarting the VPN.

### Investigation

- Parent LXC: `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1`
- Amnezia Docker container: `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0`
- Container NAT and FORWARD rules are configured correctly.
- The generated `/opt/amnezia/start.sh` configures the tunnel, iptables and MASQUERADE rules but does not enable IPv4 forwarding.
- Docker inspect shows only `net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark=1` under `HostConfig.Sysctls`.
- A fresh Docker container also defaults to forwarding disabled.
- Reproduced with two Docker versions and a completely fresh LXC installation.
- A separate installation in a full Debian VM works without manual intervention.

### Expected behavior

The official installer should explicitly enable IPv4 forwarding inside the VPN container, regardless of the default networking behavior of Docker or the host environment.

### Suggested fix

Include `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` in the Docker container's sysctl configuration alongside `net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark=1`.

Alternatively, ensure forwarding is enabled during the VPN container's initialization.

This should allow the Android app to manage installation, restarts, and updates without manual intervention.

### Impact

The installer reports success, and the VPN handshake succeeds, but all routed traffic fails. This is difficult to diagnose because the Docker container appears healthy and the client appears connected.

issues.title: Split tunneling adds local connected subnets to VPN interface routes and breaks LAN access on Windows
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**
 When split tunneling is enabled on Windows, AmneziaVPN adds local connected subnets to the VPN interface routes with metric 0.

This breaks LAN and local virtual network access because Windows routes local destinations through the VPN tunnel instead of their real local interfaces.

  Example bad routes:

  192.168.1.0/24   -> AmneziaVPN, metric 0
  192.168.1.105/32 -> AmneziaVPN, metric 0
  192.168.56.0/24  -> AmneziaVPN, metric 0
  192.168.56.1/32  -> AmneziaVPN, metric 0
  172.21.16.0/20   -> AmneziaVPN, metric 0
  172.21.16.1/32   -> AmneziaVPN, metric 0

  **To Reproduce**
  Steps to reproduce the behavior:

  1. Go to AmneziaVPN on Windows.
  2. Enable split tunneling for apps/sites.
  3. Connect to an AmneziaWG / WireGuard VPN server.
  4. Check the IPv4 route table.
  5. See that local connected subnets are routed through AmneziaVPN.
  6. Try accessing a LAN host, for example 192.168.1.1.

  Example command:

  Test-NetConnection 192.168.1.1 -Port 80

  Actual result:

  InterfaceAlias    : AmneziaVPN
  SourceAddress     : 10.8.1.6
  TcpTestSucceeded  : False

  After manually deleting the bad routes, LAN access works again:

  Remove-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix 192.168.1.0/24 -InterfaceAlias AmneziaVPN -Confirm:$false
  Remove-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix 192.168.1.105/32 -InterfaceAlias AmneziaVPN -Confirm:$false
  Remove-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix 192.168.56.0/24 -InterfaceAlias AmneziaVPN -Confirm:$false
  Remove-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix 192.168.56.1/32 -InterfaceAlias AmneziaVPN -Confirm:$false
  Remove-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix 172.21.16.0/20 -InterfaceAlias AmneziaVPN -Confirm:$false
  Remove-NetRoute -DestinationPrefix 172.21.16.1/32 -InterfaceAlias AmneziaVPN -Confirm:$false

  Then LAN routing works correctly:

  InterfaceAlias    : Wi-Fi
  SourceAddress     : 192.168.1.105
  TcpTestSucceeded  : True

  **Expected behavior**
 AmneziaVPN should not route already connected local subnets through the VPN interface when split tunneling is enabled.

  Local connected routes should keep priority and continue using their real interfaces, for example:

  192.168.1.0/24  -> Wi-Fi / Ethernet
  192.168.56.0/24 -> VirtualBox Host-Only Network
  172.21.16.0/20  -> Hyper-V vEthernet

  **Log files**
  Logs do not show route management errors. The tunnel itself appears healthy.

  Observed in logs:

  AmneziaVPN version 4.8.21.0
  Sending handshake initiation
  Received handshake response
  Sending keepalive packet

  **Screenshots**
  Not applicable.

  **Desktop:**

  - OS: Windows 11 25H2 x64
  - Version: AmneziaVPN 4.8.21.0

  **Server**

  - OS: Linux VPS

  **Additional context**
  Current settings:

  killSwitchEnabled = false
  strictKillSwitchEnabled = false
  appsSplitTunnelingEnabled = true
  sitesSplitTunnelingEnabled = true

  WFP state contains Amnezia/Mullvad split tunnel filters:

  Amnezia-SplitTunnel-Sublayer
  Mullvad Split Tunnel IPv4 Blocking Filter
  Mullvad Split Tunnel IPv4 Permissive Filter

  The tunnel daemon is started with:

  Table = off

  So these routes appear to be added by AmneziaVPN route/split-tunnel management, not directly by WireGuard.

  When split tunneling is disabled and the bad routes are manually removed, LAN works correctly while VPN internet access continues to work.

Amnezia VPN is an excellent application. However, its current distribution on privacy-oriented platforms like Linux and degoogled Android leaves much to be desired. Self-hosted: optional per-config update endpoint for in-app fleet failover/rotation
issues.body:
## Summary

An optional, opt-in improvement for self-hosted users: let a `SelfHosted` config include the operator's own update endpoint together with a pinned public key, so the client can periodically pull a refreshed config from it. This gives self-hosters automatic failover / rotation across their own fleet of servers. It is purely additive and off by default.

## Problem

Self-hosting is great, but a single server occasionally goes down — the hosting provider, a block, or just a crash. So people who self-host usually run a small fleet of servers rather than one. Today the app only understands static configs: when a server goes down, the user has to manually switch between separate configs. There is no way to do failover or rotation across your own infrastructure from inside the app.

## Proposal

Add an optional field to a self-hosted config: the operator's update endpoint plus a pinned public key. When those fields are present, the client periodically fetches a refreshed config from that endpoint, verifies the response signature against the pinned key, and applies it (server list / active server / DNS, etc.). Properties:

- **opt-in** — only active when the imported config includes these fields;
- **scoped** — only for user-imported `SelfHosted` configs;
- **verified** — the response must be signed by the key pinned at import time, so a config can only ever update itself from the operator who issued it.

In practice the operator (the self-hoster) runs a tiny endpoint that returns the current best config for their fleet, and the app follows it automatically instead of the user re-importing configs by hand.

## It fits the existing code well

*(paths/lines as of tag 4.8.19.0)*

- The `SelfHosted` config type and a per-config `api_endpoint` field already exist — [apiDefs.h (ConfigType)](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/core/api/apiDefs.h#L8-L16) and [apiEndpoint key](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/core/api/apiDefs.h#L26).
- The client already knows how to fetch a config from a remote source and apply it (containers / hostName / DNS) — [fillServerConfig()](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/ui/controllers/api/apiConfigsController.cpp#L159).
- The request base URL for those fetches is a single settable value, not hardcoded at the call sites — [Settings::setGatewayEndpoint()](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/settings.cpp#L505) — so the same fetch machinery can target a per-config endpoint.
- The architecture already supports third-party operators distributing configs through the app — the external-premium / external-trial service types in [apiUtils::getConfigType()](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client/blob/4.8.19.0/client/core/api/apiUtils.cpp#L85-L124). A self-hoster with a fleet is the same shape: they would just point at their own control plane.

## Result

Multi-server self-hosting gets real, in-app failover and rotation across your own fleet, via a small, opt-in, signature-verified mechanism that reuses machinery already present in the client. Happy to help with a PR or a test config if the direction is interesting.

---

**Reference server implementation** (runnable, clean-room, MIT): **https://github.com/wintergenius/Fleetcore** — it speaks the exact wire format this proposal implies (`GET /v1/config` → an Ed25519-signed `vpn://…` config), so the whole loop can be run with `docker run`. Details in the comment below.

**Describe the bug**

  exclusion routes for the VPN endpoint. With `0.0.0.0/1` and `128.0.0.0/1`
  pointing at the tunnel, WireGuard packets addressed to the server are routed
  back into the tunnel itself, creating a routing loop. Packets grow with each
  iteration until the socket rejects them with `sendmmsg: message too long`.

  Client 4.8.21 on the very same machine installs the routes correctly and works.
  The issue is protocol-independent — reproduced with both AmneziaWG 2.0 and 3.1
  servers.

  **To Reproduce**

  Steps to reproduce the behavior:
  1. Install 5.0.1.5 on Ubuntu 24.04 with a normal DHCP default route
  2. Connect to any AmneziaWG server
  3. Run `ip route get <server-ip>` — it points at the tunnel (`dev amn0`) instead
     of the physical gateway
  4. See `sendmmsg: message too long` in the daemon log; no traffic passes

  **Expected behavior**

  The daemon should add an exclusion route for the server endpoint through the
  physical default gateway, as 4.8.21 does:
  ```
  <server-ip> via 192.168.31.1 dev wlp0s20f3
  ```

  **Log files**

  Same 15-second window, two client versions on one machine:

  | Log line | 5.0.1.5 | 4.8.21 |
  |---|---|---|
  | `Error in received packet: Numerical argument out of domain` | 10 | 0 |
  | `No default gateway available, skipping exclusion route` | 10 | 0 |
  | exclusion routes actually installed | none | all |

5.0.1.5:
  ```
  LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for <server-ip>/32
  Error in received packet: No such file or directory
  LinuxRouteMonitor : No default gateway available, skipping exclusion route
  ...
  WireguardGo : ERROR: (amn0) peer(XXXX…) - Failed to send data packets:
                write udp 0.0.0.0:54793: sendmmsg: message too long
  ```
  
  4.8.21, same step:
  ```
  LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for <server-ip>/32
  ```
  (no warning, route present in `ip route`)
  
  Other errors present in both versions, possibly related:
  ``` 
  Error: argument "amnvpnrt" is wrong: table id value is invalid
  mkdir: cannot create directory '/sys/fs/cgroup/net_cls/amnvpnexclusions/'
  LinuxRouteMonitor : Adding exclusion route for /999999 → Invalid destination prefix
  net_cls cgroup v1 not available, traffic splitting disabled
  ```
  
  **Screenshots**
  
  N/A — the client reports "Connected".

  **Desktop (please complete the following information):**
   - OS: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (kernel 6.17), KDE Plasma / X11
   - Version: 5.0.1.5 (regression — 4.8.21 works)

  **Smartphone (please complete the following information):**
   - Not affected — mobile clients handle routing through the OS VPN API

  **Server (please complete the following information):**
   - OS: Ubuntu 24.04, Docker

**Additional context**
  
  Workaround — add the exclusion route manually before connecting:
  ```
  sudo ip route add <server-ip> via <lan-gateway> dev <iface>
  ```

  on Linux with the same `amnvpnrt` / `Invalid destination prefix` log noise.

## Describe the bug

On Windows 10, excluding `Weixin.exe` (WeChat for Windows) from the VPN using application-based split tunneling causes WeChat video calls to fail.

The VPN connection itself works correctly, and WeChat video calls succeed when application-based split tunneling is disabled or when `Weixin.exe` is not excluded.

After performing six controlled tests (A–F), I found that **adding `Weixin.exe` to the application exclusion list consistently triggers the problem**, while excluding `WeChatAppEx.exe` alone does not.

WeChat TCP connections appear to use the physical Ethernet interface when the main executable is excluded. However, the video call fails, and the observed UDP socket bindings differ from those seen during successful calls.

In some cases, the problem temporarily persists after disconnecting the VPN and fully restarting WeChat.

Important clarification: WeChat text messaging works normally in all tested configurations (A–F). I can send and receive text messages without any issues, even when Weixin.exe is excluded from the VPN. Only voice and video calls fail to connect.

This suggests that the issue specifically affects real-time calling functionality rather than general network connectivity. It may be related to UDP traffic handling, socket binding, or network interface selection, although the exact cause has not yet been confirmed.

1. On Windows 10, install AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 and connect to a self-hosted VPN server.

6. Connect to the VPN.

8. Start a new WeChat voice or video call.

**Describe the bug**

The AmneziaWG connection built into AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 fails on Windows 11 26H2.

The tunnel interface is created successfully, but the client cannot send or receive UDP packets. The service log repeatedly reports errors from `WSASendMsg` and `WSARecvMsg`:

```text
wsasendmsg: The system detected an invalid pointer address in attempting to use a pointer argument in a call.

wsarecvmsg: The system detected an invalid pointer address in attempting to use a pointer argument in a call.
```

As a result, the AmneziaWG handshake never completes.

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN: 5.0.3.0
- Windows: Windows 11 26H2
- Windows build: 26300
- Architecture: x64
- Wintun: 0.14
- Protocol: AmneziaWG
- Standalone AmneziaWG for Windows: 3.1.0

## Troubleshooting performed

I tried the following without success:

- Rebooted the laptop
- Disabled split tunneling
- Disabled Kill Switch
- Confirmed that ByeDPI and Zapret are not installed
- Confirmed that DNS settings are obtained automatically through DHCP
- Flushed and renewed the network configuration
- Checked the Winsock catalog
- Checked installed network filters
- Confirmed that AdGuard and other third-party Winsock providers are not installed

The same AmneziaWG configuration works correctly:

- On a mobile phone connected to the same Wi-Fi network
- In standalone AmneziaWG for Windows 3.1.0 on the same laptop

## Additional observations

AmneziaVPN automatically sets the tunnel MTU to 1376. The failure occurs before the first UDP handshake packet can be sent, so changing the MTU or DNS settings does not appear relevant.

Standalone AmneziaWG 3.1.0 works correctly with exactly the same configuration on the same Windows installation.

This strongly suggests a regression or incompatibility in the AmneziaWG tunnel implementation bundled with AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 on Windows 11 26H2.

issues.title: [macOS][VLESS] Split tunnel exclusion for connected LAN subnet routes via router and breaks LAN access
issues.body:
## Summary

On macOS, AmneziaVPN site-based split tunneling in “Addresses from the list should not be accessed via VPN” mode breaks access to a directly connected LAN subnet when that subnet is added to the exclusion list. The client installs the subnet route via the LAN router instead of on-link via Wi-Fi.

## Environment

- macOS 27.0 (26A428), Wi-Fi `en0`
- AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0 and 5.0.2.1 macOS `.pkg` builds (both reproduced)
- Amnezia Premium, VLESS/XRay connection
- LAN: `192.168.31.0/24`; Mac: `192.168.31.105`; router: `192.168.31.1`
- Site-based split tunneling enabled, “Addresses from the list should not be accessed via VPN”, with `192.168.31.0/24` in the list

## Reproduction

1. Connect Wi-Fi on `192.168.31.0/24` and confirm a LAN host such as `192.168.31.47` is reachable directly.
2. Add `192.168.31.0/24` to site-based split tunneling exclusions and connect VLESS.
3. Run `netstat -rn -f inet`, `route -n get 192.168.31.47`, and `ping 192.168.31.47`.

## Actual

The client creates this route:

```text
192.168.31/24  192.168.31.1  UGSc  en0
```

The LAN host does not answer. An Ethernet capture on `en0` shows ICMP packets for `192.168.31.47` sent to the router's MAC address, not the LAN host's MAC. The router can return `Destination Port Unreachable`.

Removing `192.168.31.0/24` from the exclusion list removes the bad gateway route, but traffic for the LAN subnet then follows the VPN `/1` route and the host remains unreachable. A temporary direct on-link route for the subnet through `en0` immediately restores ping and ARP resolution of the LAN host. All temporary routes were removed after diagnosis.

## Expected

The connected `192.168.31.0/24` subnet should remain reachable on-link through `en0` while the VPN is connected. If explicitly excluded, the client should not route same-subnet packets through `192.168.31.1`.

## Related reports

- #2830 reports a different Windows route-capture problem affecting connected LAN subnets.
- #2937 / #2973 concern loss of CIDR prefix during input normalization; the full `/24` is present in the route here, so this is separate.
